Now that we've isolated the traffic and completely purged the fake security software from the theater's workstations, the manager wants us to establish a long-term defense framework. We need to prevent the staff from falling for these malicious browser pop-ups ever again. What is the most effective proactive countermeasure we should implement?

options.optionText: Accept the retainer contract to perform continuous browser hardening audits and build custom security training for their branch locations.
Politely decline the long-term contract, collect the immediate payout for today's emergency clean-up, and clear our queue for the next threat alert.

Management is thrilled with our incident response and just processed our payout. They also asked if we could stay on retainer to audit their main corporate ticketing network next month. What's our play?

pointsOfInterest.title: Urgent Payroll Text
pointsOfInterest.description: A payroll-themed SMS claims an employee's deposit will fail unless they verify immediately. The pressure is the point: urgency makes people move before they inspect the link.

pointsOfInterest.title: Helpdesk Pretext
pointsOfInterest.description: A caller says they are from internal IT and asks an employee to read a one-time code aloud. A convincing role is not proof of authority.

decisions.optionText: Tell the employee to end the call and verify through the official helpdesk channel.
Let the caller continue because they know the employee's full name.

pointsOfInterest.title: Swapped QR Sticker
pointsOfInterest.description: A cafe table has a fresh QR sticker placed over the real menu code. Physical placement can make a malicious link feel ordinary.

pointsOfInterest.title: Fake Delivery DM
pointsOfInterest.description: A social media message claims a parcel is stuck and asks for a small redelivery fee. The amount is tiny, but the form harvests payment details.

decisions.optionText: Check the order through the official delivery site instead of the message link.
Pay the fee quickly because the message says the package expires today.

pointsOfInterest.title: Lobby Tailgate
pointsOfInterest.description: Someone carrying boxes asks an employee to hold the secure door open. Politeness is valuable, but access control still needs verification.

pointsOfInterest.title: Parking Lot USB
pointsOfInterest.description: A USB drive labeled 'Salary Review' appears near an office entrance. Curiosity is a classic baiting trigger, especially when the label feels personal.

decisions.optionText: Turn it over to security for controlled analysis without plugging it in.
Open it on a personal laptop to see who lost it.

pointsOfInterest.title: Vendor Invoice Switch
pointsOfInterest.description: An invoice arrives from a known vendor, but the bank account number has changed. Business email compromise often hides inside routine paperwork.

pointsOfInterest.title: Calendar Lure
pointsOfInterest.description: A meeting invite appears with a link titled 'Updated benefits packet.' Calendar spam feels official because it lands directly in the user's schedule.

decisions.optionText: Report the invite, remove it, and adjust calendar settings to block automatic additions.
Open the packet because it is already on the calendar.

pointsOfInterest.title: Look-Alike Handle
pointsOfInterest.description: A fake brand account uses one extra letter and the same profile picture as the real account. Visual familiarity can hide tiny identity changes.

pointsOfInterest.title: Synthetic Voice Mail
pointsOfInterest.description: A short voice message sounds like an executive asking for a rushed transfer. Deepfake audio raises the value of out-of-band confirmation.

decisions.optionText: Pause the request and confirm it through a separate trusted contact path.
Approve the transfer because the voice sounds familiar.

pointsOfInterest.title: Polished Fake App
pointsOfInterest.description: A fake utility app has clean screenshots, glowing reviews, and a name close to a trusted product. Professional presentation is not verification.

pointsOfInterest.title: Train Station Screen
pointsOfInterest.description: A commuter opens an admin panel on a crowded platform. Social engineering is not always a message; sometimes it starts with someone simply watching.

decisions.optionText: Recommend privacy screens and a habit of avoiding sensitive work in exposed spaces.
Photograph the screen to prove the exposure happened.

pointsOfInterest.title: Crisis Charity Scam
pointsOfInterest.description: A donation page appears minutes after breaking news and asks for mobile wallet payments. Emotional timing is a powerful social engineering tool.

pointsOfInterest.title: Manipulation Pattern Review
pointsOfInterest.description: Urgency, authority, curiosity, fear, generosity, and convenience all appear in different attacks. Spotting the emotion being pushed is often the first defensive clue.
